## Part 0: Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| results: hide
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)
library(spdep)
library(nngeo)
library(gt)
options(scipen = 999, timeout = 300, tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = 160)
dollars <- scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)
percent <- scales::label_percent(accuracy = .1)
dir.create("data/assignment5/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
save_plot <- function(plot, name, width = 8, height = 5) {
  ggsave(file.path("data/assignment5/figures", paste0(name, ".png")), plot,
         width = width, height = height, dpi = 160, bg = "white")

}
```

**Team:** Mahjong.

### Data preparation

We combine the supplied house characteristics with location and recent-crime
features, then compare the models using the same ten validation folds.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-and-fit
#| results: hide
source("data/assignment5/prepare_features.R", local = TRUE)
source("data/assignment5/fit_models.R", local = TRUE)
final_row <- model_log %>% filter(model == final_name)
original_row <- model_log %>% filter(model == "m10")
ward_lot_row <- model_log %>% filter(model == "E3")
```

The final model allows the lot-area coefficient to differ between northern and
southern locations. Its
mean-fold CV RMSE is **`r dollars(final_row$cv_rmse)`**. The analysis below compares
its prediction errors and income-group valuation ratios with the earlier models.

## Part 1: Clean and explore

### Market-sale sample

We screen out training transfers at or below $10,000, multiple-property sales,
and records without positive building area or valid coordinates. A transaction
covering several properties does not identify the value of the one house whose
features are recorded. There is no upper-price or upper-age cutoff. All test
records remain, and missing predictors are filled inside each training fold.

```{r}
#| label: cleaning-log
features$cleaning_log %>% gt() %>%
  cols_label(rule = "Rule", reason = "Reason", removed = "Removed", remaining = "Remaining") %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(removed, remaining), decimals = 0)
```

The rules retain **`r scales::comma(nrow(train_raw))` training sales** out of 23,200.
All 1,232 actual exclusions are multiple-property transactions; the other rules
remove no records in these supplied files. We predict all
**`r scales::comma(nrow(test_raw))` test houses**. The test set still includes
**`r sum(test_raw$is_multisale == 1)` multiple-property transactions**, so CV on
retained single-property sales does not directly validate that subgroup.

### Exploration

```{r}
#| label: price-distribution
#| fig-alt: "Distribution of retained training prices on a logarithmic dollar axis."
p_price <- ggplot(train_raw, aes(sale_price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 45, fill = "#2c7fb8", color = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Sale prices have a long upper tail", x = "Sale price (log axis)", y = "Sales")
save_plot(p_price, "price_distribution")
```

The plot uses a log axis for display; the regression outcome stays in dollars.

```{r}
#| label: price-map
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-alt: "Chicago retained training sales colored by price."
p_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = features$wards, fill = "#f7f7f7", color = "#cccccc", linewidth = .15) +
  geom_sf(data = train_raw, aes(color = sale_price), size = .35, alpha = .7) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = scales::label_dollar(), name = "Price", option = "C") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) + labs(title = "Location is strongly associated with price") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
save_plot(p_map, "price_map", height = 7)
```

```{r}
#| label: size-price
#| fig-alt: "Building area and training sale price, with a descriptive quadratic curve."
p_size <- ggplot(train_raw, aes(building_000sf, sale_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .18, size = .7, color = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "#b35806") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "m")) +
  labs(title = "Larger houses have a wider range of prices", x = "Building area (1,000 sq ft)", y = "Price")
save_plot(p_size, "size_price")
```

```{r}
#| label: age-price
#| fig-alt: "Median price by decade of age, with all houses age 150 and older pooled."
age_summary <- train_raw %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(age_bin = if_else(building_age >= 150, 150, floor(building_age / 10) * 10)) %>%
  group_by(age_bin) %>% summarize(n = n(), median_price = median(sale_price), .groups = "drop")
p_age <- ggplot(age_summary, aes(age_bin, median_price)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2c7fb8") + geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 150, 30),
    labels = function(x) ifelse(x == 150, "150+", as.character(x))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Age patterns are nonlinear, but the oldest tail is sparse",
       x = "Age group (start of decade)", y = "Median price", size = "Sales")
save_plot(p_age, "age_price")
```

There is only one sale in the original 170–179-year group. We pool ages 150 and
above for display so that one transaction is not presented as a stable age trend.
No old houses are removed from modeling. The descriptive tail alone does not justify a quadratic specification.

The price map motivates place effects. The area plot motivates nonlinear terms
and location-specific area slopes. We also examine low-income overvaluation using out-of-fold predictions.
We retain legitimate expensive houses because they are part of the prediction
task and can strongly affect dollar RMSE.

## Part 2: Build the model

### Predictors and validation

| Feature | Construction |
|---|---|
| House structure | Area, age, lot size, bedrooms, bathrooms, fireplace, garage, air conditioning, stories, basement, exterior and furnace |
| Transformations | Log lot area; squared area, age and downtown distance |
| Time | Year and quarter indicators |
| Broad location | Distance and east/north coordinates relative to downtown |
| Ward | 2023 Ward fixed effects and area-by-Ward interactions; sparse Wards merged geographically |
| Robbery exposure | Log count within 660 ft and log mean distance to five recent events |
| North/South | Main effect and log-lot interaction at projected `north_mi = 0` |

Ward boundaries are the 2023 geography. Crime features use events from 2023–2025
in the preceding available complete quarter, ending at least seven days before
sale. Early-2023 houses have unavailable crime history within the allowed window;
their values are imputed and flagged. The current historical crime extract may
include later revisions: an earlier event date does not establish that the same
record version was available at sale time. Income is only a retrospective diagnostic.

We use the original fixed ten folds (seed 5080), grouping identical coordinates.
All models use identical retained rows, folds and five-neighbor row-standardized
spatial weights. Imputation medians are learned only in each analysis fold. No features use neighboring prices, held-out prices or residuals.

### Sequential model development

Models m1–m10 form a step-by-step sequence. Each model adds or changes predictors
in the preceding model, starting with house characteristics in m1 and ending
with the original full model, m10.

```{r}
#| label: original-model-log
model_log %>% filter(model %in% paste0("m", 1:10)) %>%
  select(model, added, cv_rmse, moran_i, notes) %>% gt() %>%
  cols_label(model = "Model", added = "Added / changed", cv_rmse = "CV RMSE",
    moran_i = "Moran's I", notes = "Reason") %>%
  fmt_currency(columns = cv_rmse, decimals = 0) %>% fmt_number(columns = moran_i, decimals = 4)
```

### Alternative model specifications

These models test separate alternatives rather than a sequence of additions.
E1–E4 each modify m10. NS adds a North/South indicator and a log-lot-area
interaction to m10, allowing the lot-area coefficient to differ by region.

```{r}
#| label: alternative-model-log
model_log %>% filter(startsWith(model, "E") | model == "NS") %>%
  select(model, added, cv_rmse, moran_i, notes) %>% gt() %>%
  cols_label(model = "Model", added = "Added / changed", cv_rmse = "CV RMSE",
    moran_i = "Moran's I", notes = "Reason") %>%
  fmt_currency(columns = cv_rmse, decimals = 0) %>% fmt_number(columns = moran_i, decimals = 4)
```

## Part 3: Final model

The selected model is **NS**, with mean-fold RMSE **`r dollars(final_row$cv_rmse)`**
and pooled OOF RMSE **`r dollars(final_row$pooled_oof_rmse)`**. Its mean-fold RMSE
is **`r percent(1 - final_row$cv_rmse / original_row$cv_rmse)`** lower than original m10
and **`r percent(1 - final_row$cv_rmse / model_log$cv_rmse[model_log$model == 'm1'])`**
lower than the structure-only baseline. These two RMSE summaries have different
aggregation rules and are labeled separately.

```{r}
#| label: comparison-table
comparison %>% select(model, cv_rmse, pooled_oof_rmse, moran_i,
                      oof_negative, test_negative, test_min) %>% gt() %>%
  cols_label(model = "Model", cv_rmse = "Mean-fold RMSE", pooled_oof_rmse = "Pooled RMSE",
    moran_i = "Moran's I", oof_negative = "OOF negatives", test_negative = "Test negatives",
    test_min = "Minimum test prediction") %>%
  fmt_currency(columns = c(cv_rmse, pooled_oof_rmse, test_min), decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = moran_i, decimals = 4)
```

NS reduces RMSE and residual clustering compared with m10, and decreases negative
predictions from 56 to 10 in cross-validation and from 12 to 2 in the test set.
E3 has a lower RMSE but produces an extreme negative test prediction of about
**`r dollars(ward_lot_row$test_min)`**. We choose NS as a simpler geographic adjustment,
while recognizing that its low-income valuation ratios are slightly worse than m10's.

```{r}
#| label: final-formula
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
# Predict sale price in dollars; R includes an intercept by default.
f_final <- sale_price ~
  # Building area (1,000 sq ft) and age (decades).
  building_000sf + age_decade +
  # Room counts, amenities, and building characteristics.
  num_bedrooms + num_full_baths + num_half_baths +
  num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story +
  full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace +
  # Natural log of lot area; squared terms allow curved area and age effects.
  log_lot + I(building_000sf^2) + I(age_decade^2) +
  # Sale-year and quarter indicators capture market changes and seasonality.
  year_f + quarter_f +
  # Distance to downtown and signed east/north coordinates, in miles.
  downtown_mi + I(downtown_mi^2) + east_mi + north_mi +
  # Ward indicators allow different baseline prices across Wards.
  model_ward +
  # log(1 + nearby robbery count), unavailable-history flag,
  # and log(1 + mean distance to the five nearest recent robberies).
  log_robbery + crime_unavailable + log_knn5 +
  # North/South indicator allows different regional baseline prices.
  lot_zone +
  # The area coefficient may differ across Wards.
  building_000sf:model_ward +
  # The area coefficient may change with building age.
  building_000sf:age_decade +
  # The log-lot coefficient may differ between North and South.
  log_lot:lot_zone
```

The North/South boundary is fixed at `north_mi = 0`, relative to downtown.
Both regions are estimated in one regression. The interaction allows the log-lot
coefficient to differ between regions while sharing the other model terms.

```{r}
#| label: selected-coefficients
all_coefficients[[final_name]] %>% filter(term %in% c("num_full_baths", "num_bedrooms",
  "log_lot", "lot_zoneSouth", "log_lot:lot_zoneSouth", "building_000sf:age_decade")) %>%
  gt() %>% fmt_number(columns = estimate, decimals = 1)
bath_coefficient <- coef(m_final)[["num_full_baths"]]
```

### Baseline and final residual maps

```{r}
#| label: residual-maps
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-alt: "Structure-only baseline and final North/South model out-of-fold residuals on the same color scale."
residual_map <- bind_rows(
  diagnostics %>% select(id) %>% mutate(model = "Structure-only baseline (m1)", residual = diagnostics$residual_baseline),
  diagnostics %>% select(id) %>% mutate(model = "Final North/South model (NS)", residual = diagnostics$residual_final)) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("Structure-only baseline (m1)", "Final North/South model (NS)")))
p_residual <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = features$wards, fill = "#f7f7f7", color = "#cccccc", linewidth = .1) +
  geom_sf(data = residual_map, aes(color = residual), size = .3, alpha = .65) +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "#f7f7f7", high = "#b2182b",
    limits = c(-500000, 500000), breaks = c(-500000, 0, 500000), oob = scales::squish,
    labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"), name = "Actual - predicted",
    guide = guide_colorbar(barwidth = grid::unit(9, "cm"), title.position = "top")) +
  facet_wrap(~model) + coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "Place features reduce, but do not remove, spatial errors",
    caption = "Red: underprediction. Blue: overprediction. Colors capped at +/-$500,000.") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid = element_blank())
save_plot(p_residual, "residual_maps", width = 10, height = 7)
```

Moran's I falls from **`r sprintf('%.3f', original_row$moran_i)`** for m10 to
**`r sprintf('%.3f', final_row$moran_i)`** for NS. Positive residual clustering remains;
this statistic describes spatial errors, not a significance test.

## Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays

### 4A. Largest errors

```{r}
#| label: geographic-errors
error_by_ward <- diagnostics %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% group_by(ward) %>%
  summarize(sales = n(), rmse = sqrt(mean(residual_final^2)),
    mean_residual = mean(residual_final), median_price = median(sale_price), .groups = "drop")
worst_ward <- error_by_ward %>% filter(sales >= 50) %>% arrange(desc(rmse)) %>% slice(1)
error_by_ward %>% filter(sales >= 50) %>% arrange(desc(rmse)) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>%
  gt() %>% fmt_currency(columns = c(rmse, mean_residual, median_price), decimals = 0)
```

Ward **`r worst_ward$ward`** has the largest OOF RMSE among Wards with at least
50 retained sales: **`r dollars(worst_ward$rmse)`**. Its mean residual is
**`r dollars(worst_ward$mean_residual)`**. Mean errors can cancel even where individual
errors are large. Unmeasured renovation, interior quality and unusual luxury
properties are plausible sources of remaining errors; these diagnostics do not
identify their causes.

```{r}
#| label: largest-errors
largest_errors <- diagnostics %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(residual_final))) %>% slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  select(id, ward, sale_price, pred_final, residual_final)
largest_errors %>% gt() %>%
  fmt_currency(columns = c(sale_price, pred_final, residual_final), decimals = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: observed-predicted
#| fig-alt: "Actual versus out-of-fold final predictions with a 45-degree reference line."
p_fit <- ggplot(diagnostics, aes(sale_price, pred_final)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = 2, color = "#555555") +
  geom_point(alpha = .25, size = .8, color = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "m")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "m")) +
  coord_equal() + labs(title = "The final model still misses unusual properties",
    x = "Observed price", y = "Out-of-fold prediction")
save_plot(p_fit, "observed_predicted")
```

### 4B. Neighborhood income and valuation ratios

Tract median income is from the 2023 ACS five-year table B19013 (2019–2023).
Because those estimates were released after some sales, they are used only for
retrospective equity diagnostics, not as predictors. The **`r sum(is.na(diagnostics$income_group))`**
records without a valid income group remain in the regression and are omitted
only from the income comparison.

```{r}
#| label: income-summary
income_summary <- income_metrics %>% filter(model %in% c("m10", "NS"))
income_summary %>% select(model, income_group, n, median_ratio, mean_ratio, share_overvalued) %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "model") %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(median_ratio, mean_ratio), decimals = 3) %>%
  fmt_percent(columns = share_overvalued, decimals = 1)
```

The low-income median ratio rises from **`r sprintf('%.3f', original_row$low_income_median_ratio)`**
to **`r sprintf('%.3f', final_row$low_income_median_ratio)`**, and the overvalued share rises
from **`r percent(original_row$low_income_overvalued)`** to **`r percent(final_row$low_income_overvalued)`**.
Thus, better overall RMSE does not improve this equity diagnostic. The low-income
mean ratio is **`r sprintf('%.3f', final_row$low_income_mean_ratio)`**. These ratios describe
neighborhood income groups, not individual owners' incomes.

```{r}
#| label: income-ratios
#| fig-alt: "Median valuation ratios for original m10 and final North/South across income groups."
p_income <- income_summary %>% mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("m10", "NS"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(income_group, median_ratio, color = model, group = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("m10" = "#777777", "NS" = "#2166ac")) +
  labs(title = "Lower-income neighborhoods remain overvalued",
    x = "Tract median household income", y = "Median predicted / sale price", color = "Model") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
save_plot(p_income, "income_ratios")
```

```{r}
#| label: cleaning-by-income
cleaning_by_income <- features$all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% filter(split == "train") %>%
  mutate(income_group = cut(income, c(-Inf, 50000, 75000, 100000, Inf),
    labels = levels(diagnostics$income_group))) %>% filter(!is.na(income_group)) %>%
  group_by(income_group) %>% summarize(original_sales = n(), excluded = sum(exclusion != "Retained"),
    excluded_share = mean(exclusion != "Retained"),
    retained_under_50k = sum(exclusion == "Retained" & sale_price < 50000), .groups = "drop")
cleaning_by_income %>% gt() %>% fmt_percent(columns = excluded_share, decimals = 1)
```

The comparison describes retained single-property sales. Raising the price
cutoff would hide some low-price homes with large proportional errors, rather
than demonstrating improved valuation. [The Tax Divide](https://www.propublica.org/series/the-tax-divide)
documented disproportionate assessments on lower-value properties. Our model also overvalues lower-income neighborhoods and does not resolve this disparity. Holding tax
rates and exemptions constant, overvaluation raises an owner's share of the tax burden.

## Part 5: Predict the test houses

```{r}
#| label: predict-test
# Refit the selected formula and the complete feature recipe on all retained training sales.
recipe_final <- learn_recipe(train_raw)
train <- prepare(train_raw, recipe_final)
test <- prepare(test_raw, recipe_final)
m_final <- lm(f_final, train, na.action = na.fail)
preds <- tibble(id = test$id, pred = as.numeric(predict(m_final, test)))
stopifnot(identical(preds$id, read_csv("data/assignment5/chicago_test.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)$id),
  nrow(preds) == 5789L, !anyDuplicated(preds$id), all(is.finite(preds$pred)))
write_csv(preds, "assignments/team_Mahjong_predictions.csv")
write_csv(preds, "data/assignment5/assignment5_predictions.csv")
tibble(test_rows = nrow(preds), finite_predictions = sum(is.finite(preds$pred)),
       negative_predictions = sum(preds$pred < 0)) %>% knitr::kable()
```

**Final mean-fold CV RMSE: `r dollars(final_row$cv_rmse)`.**
**Pooled OOF RMSE: `r dollars(final_row$pooled_oof_rmse)`.**
Predictions for all 5,789 test houses are exported to
**[`team_Mahjong_predictions.csv`](team_Mahjong_predictions.csv)**. The test set has no observed prices, so its
RMSE cannot be calculated before instructor scoring.

```{r}
#| label: negative-test-case
negative_test %>% gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(lotsize_acre, building_000sf), decimals = 4) %>%
  fmt_currency(columns = pred, decimals = 0)
```

Two test predictions remain negative. We retain these values in the output and
report them as a limitation of the linear model. The test sample includes
multiple-property sales and a house larger than any retained training property,
so some predictions extend beyond the population represented in validation.

## Part 6: Reflection

Location was the most useful source of improvement. Adding Ward effects and
allowing the building-area coefficient to vary across Wards substantially
reduced prediction error. The final North/South adjustment then allowed the
relationship between lot area and price to differ across two broad regions.
It improved RMSE and reduced negative predictions without requiring a separate
regression for every neighborhood. These are predictive associations, not proof
that geography itself causes the price differences.

The model comparisons also show why RMSE alone is insufficient. Ward-specific
lot-area slopes achieved a lower error but generated an extreme negative test
prediction. We preferred the broader North/South adjustment, which produced
fewer negative values. Nevertheless, two negative test predictions remain, and
unusual houses are still difficult to value. Valid expensive and old houses
were retained because removing them would change the population being predicted.

The full-bathroom coefficient is **`r dollars(bath_coefficient)`**. Holding the other
predictors fixed, one additional full bathroom changes the fitted price by this
amount. This does not measure the causal return from adding a bathroom: interior
condition, renovation and other unrecorded features may also explain the association.

The equity results are less encouraging. Although NS improves overall dollar
accuracy, the lowest-income group's median valuation ratio and overvalued share
increase slightly relative to m10. We therefore cannot describe the final model
as an improvement in assessment fairness. If used for taxation, its remaining
proportional errors could place excess burden on owners of lower-valued homes.

We would use these predictions to support review, not to set tax bills directly.
Additional condition data may help, but any changes should be assessed using
both accuracy and income-group diagnostics. Repeated comparisons on the same
folds can make the chosen CV result optimistic. Hidden test prices provide a
separate check, while prediction for future years would require time-based validation.

### AI Team Statement

Our team uses AI as a supporting tool for coding, data preparation, and communication. Team members remain responsible for the analysis, model choices, interpretation of results, and final submission.

For this assignment, we used Codex to assist with writing and debugging R code, implementing feature engineering and model comparisons, and locating, collecting, and preparing external data. We also used AI to help polish the explanation.
